facts.text: Designed as an inward-facing space to mask the sight and sound of the Embarcadero Freeway.
The Vaillancourt fountain was installed in 1971.
Began as a corporate garden gifted to San Francisco by Esprit Corporation.
Reopened after renovation with separate dog and people areas.
The softball field is named for Rikki Streicher, a founder of the Gay Olympics; a plaque was dedicated in 1996.
The gymnasium was named for Mark Bingham in 2002.
Has a sandbox and a separate gated playground with soft rubber flooring for small children.
Also has a basketball court, a lighted tennis court and a baseball field.

name: Fairmount Open Space
note: Source calls it Fairmount Plaza; sfrecpark lists it as Fairmont Plaza.

facts.text: A hilltop open space with paths, box steps and a lookout between Fairmount Heights and Diamond Heights.
Restored from a thicket of dying eucalyptus with hundreds of native plants such as yarrow, California sage and lupine.
The post was renamed Fort Mason in 1882 to honor Colonel Richard Barnes Mason.
Served as headquarters of the San Francisco Port of Embarkation during both world wars.
Built on the site of the Francisco Reservoir, constructed in 1859.
Opened to the public on April 27, 2022.
Built by the Francisco Park Conservancy and then transferred to the Recreation and Park Department.
Has an athletic field, outdoor fitness equipment, a picnic area and a playground.
Has a sheltered sand playground, basketball and tennis courts and picnic tables.
The clubhouse runs an after-school program, teen nights and tiny tots classes.
Has a swimming pool, athletic field, playground and courts.
The pool and clubhouse building was renovated and reopened in 2021.

name: George and Judy Marcus Garden of Enchantment
note: Garden at the de Young Museum in Golden Gate Park.

facts.text: Has gazebos covered in spiraling grapevines and a pond with water lilies.
Features a metal sculpture, Untitled (Pirate) from 2007, facing the pond.
Named for George Christopher, the 34th mayor of San Francisco.
Has a playground, softball field, tennis courts and basketball courts.
Named for poet George Sterling, who was called the unofficial poet laureate of San Francisco.
A historical marker with a panel of Sterling's poetry was erected in 2005 by Friends of Sterling Park and Russian Hill Neighbors.
Has an outdoor basketball court, a baseball diamond, a playground and outdoor fitness equipment.
A 66.6-acre recreation area with hiking trails and open space.
The land was once Adolph Sutro's Gum Tree Ranch and later a Crocker Real Estate Company picnic site and amusement park.
Combines a playground, tennis court and lawns with a hilltop dune showing San Francisco dune plant life.
The play equipment includes a net climbing structure.
A hilltop park with a dune plant community atop 140-million-year-old Franciscan chert.

name: Grandview Open Space
note: Same hill as Grandview Park; facts from the Grandview Park page.

facts.text: A 0.2-mile trail climbs to the hilltop, mostly on wooden stairs.
Has a renovated soccer field, two tennis courts and a basketball court.
Home to the non-profit Haight Ashbury Community Nursery School.

name: Harding Park
note: Now TPC Harding Park Golf Course.

facts.text: Named for President Warren G. Harding and opened on July 18, 1925.
The original 18-hole course was designed by Willie Watson and Sam Whiting.
A quarter-acre playground and clubhouse with a community room, basketball and tennis courts and outdoor fitness equipment.

name: Helen Wills Park
note: Listed by sfrecpark as Helen Wills Playground, Broadway and Larkin.

facts.text: Has a multi-functional clubhouse, sports courts and its own boardwalk.
Its EcoCenter serves as a classroom for local schools and community groups.
Its Nature Exploration Area won UNICEF's 2021 Cities Inspires Award.
Has a bay overlook, a large community lawn and a reservable picnic area.
Has a 70-foot sundial whose base forms a stage for a surrounding amphitheater.
The city's first public skateboard park, and the skate bowl is still in use.
